Prone positioning involves placing a patient on his or her chest and abdomen to reduce airway resistance and improve ventilation. It can significantly impact ventilator settings for patients with severe lung injury in several ways:

1. Pressure-limited tidal volume: In this approach, the target tidal volume is set as a fraction of the patient’s predicted body weight or ideal body weight. The inspiratory pressure is increased until the target tidal volume is reached, making it pressure-limited.

2. Permissive hypercapnia: This is usually acceptable when prone positioning is applied. Increased carbon dioxide levels can occur due to the high ventilation-to-perfusion mismatch observed in the dorsal regions of lung injury when the supine position is used.

3. PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) titration: PEEP is often adjusted based on the changes in lung compliance during prone position. Higher levels of PEEP are usually applied during prone position to maintain alveolar recruitment in the dorsal zones of the lungs.

4. Volume control: Prone positioning can change ventilator settings that rely on measuring air flow and volume. As such, it becomes imperative to adjust the settings in the early stages of the intervention to keep up with changes in ventilation and perfusion throughout the lung.

Prone positioning has been shown to improve oxygenation and survival rates in patients with severe acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). It is generally accepted as an effective rescue therapy for those with refractory hypoxemia despite appropriate treatment with supine positioning.
